id: The Zebra Goes Wild Where the Sidewalk Ends

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Neon stripes tighten my wall where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My black father sits crooked in the kitchen drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor he curses the landlord who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking his soul. II Chains of light race over my stricken city. Glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris I will recall my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb. In America all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and ibm spark: let us program rabies. the madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra is gone into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming and my father on the specimen table.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text depicts racial oppression, poverty, and dehumanization in America through surreal, violent imagery of a Black father, a predatory landlord, and mechanized urban power. It finds that Black life is trapped, exploited, and stripped of freedom, making the poem a stark indictment of systemic racism and social control.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Neon, Jesus, Chains

outputs.L1:
I

Neon stripes tighten around my wall, where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My Black father sits crooked in the kitchen, drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor, he curses the landlord, who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking his soul.

II

Chains of light race over my stricken city—a glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena, where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris, I will remember my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb.

In America, all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and IBM spark: Let us program rabies. The madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra is gone into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming, and my father on the specimen table.
outputs.L2:
I  
Bright bands of neon squeeze across my wall, beneath the place where my landlord’s crayon image dangles from a twisted nail. In the kitchen, my Black father slumps unevenly, intoxicated by the blood of Jesus changed into low-priced wine. Shaking, he denounces the landlord, whose smile peers out from the pages of the rent ledger. My father’s eyes resemble cotton pods. He is positioned on the landlord’s surgical slab, while the country’s needle drains away his spirit.

II  
Ropes of brightness speed through my damaged city. A shining net has been woven by the pale widow spider. I look upon this fierce spectacle, a place where foreign electric darkness has strapped us in. Even after daylight rinses the wreckage clean, I will remember the landlord suspended in my room and my father groaning inside Christ’s grave. In America, every zebra is caged in a zoo. I hear engines snap and IBM circuits flare: let us code the disease of madness. The frenzy is already frothing. No untamed zebras cross the American fields. The rabid dogs are loose. The African zebra has vanished into dust. I watch the stealers of shadows approach, and I see my father laid out on the examination table.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a powerful vision of oppression by turning the figure of the landlord into a symbol of rent, control, and social domination. The landlord is not simply an individual who owns property; he represents a larger system that traps poor Black people in conditions of dependency and fear. Through this image, the poem shows how housing becomes a tool of power, where the threat of eviction, debt, and economic pressure limits freedom and reinforces inequality.

The speaker also portrays the father as a deeply wounded figure, broken down by forces beyond his control. Poverty has weakened him materially, racism has damaged his dignity and opportunities, alcohol appears as both an escape and a symptom of suffering, and religion is connected not with comfort but with pain and endurance. The father’s suffering is therefore personal, but it is also historical and social. He becomes an example of how oppressive systems destroy individuals from within, shaping their bodies, emotions, and beliefs.

The city in the poem is depicted as a hostile and mechanized environment. Rather than being a place of community or possibility, it appears cold, artificial, and threatening. It is dominated by white power and by forms of technology that alienate rather than liberate. Machines, institutions, and urban structures seem to reduce human beings to objects or functions. In this setting, Black life is surrounded by forces that monitor, exploit, and control it.

The poem also connects Black suffering in America to a longer history of captivity and exploitation. The speaker’s images suggest that the pain experienced in the present is linked to the loss of African freedom through slavery, displacement, and colonial violence. America is shown not as a place of true liberation, but as a continuation of captivity in new forms. Economic exploitation, racial domination, and cultural disconnection all become part of the same historical wound.

Finally, the repeated images of medical experimentation, programming, and manipulation suggest a world in which Black people are treated as objects rather than human beings. These images create a sense of systemic dehumanization: people are studied, controlled, conditioned, or “programmed” by institutions that claim authority over their bodies and minds. The result is a vision of social madness, where the real insanity lies not in the oppressed, but in the society that produces such suffering. Through these images, the poem condemns the structures that distort human life and expose the violence hidden beneath everyday systems of power.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a bleak and unsettling vision of Black life in America, using surreal and violent imagery to expose the forces of racial oppression, poverty, and dehumanization. At its center is the figure of a Black father whose suffering is not only personal but also symbolic. He represents generations of Black people forced to endure economic hardship, social humiliation, and physical vulnerability in a society structured against them. His body and identity are placed under pressure by forces larger than himself, suggesting that racism is not an isolated act of cruelty but a system that shapes everyday life.

The landlord appears as a predatory figure, representing economic exploitation and the power of property over the poor. Rather than offering shelter or security, the landlord becomes part of the machinery of oppression. Housing, which should provide safety and dignity, is transformed into another means of control. Through this figure, the text shows how poverty is maintained by those who profit from the desperation of others. The Black family is not simply poor by accident; they are trapped within a social order that extracts money, labor, and dignity from them while giving little in return.

The poem’s urban imagery also contributes to its sense of entrapment. The city is not portrayed as a place of opportunity or freedom, but as a mechanized and hostile environment. Its power seems cold, impersonal, and violent, as though the city itself has become a machine designed to crush human life. This imagery suggests that oppression is built into the structures of modern society: housing systems, labor systems, policing, and economic institutions all work together to restrict Black existence. The result is a world in which people are treated less like human beings than like objects to be used, controlled, or discarded.

The surreal quality of the text intensifies this critique. By exaggerating violence and distortion, the poem reveals the emotional truth of systemic racism. The strange and nightmarish images do not take the reader away from reality; instead, they make reality more visible. They show how racism and poverty can make ordinary life feel grotesque, terrifying, and absurd. The father’s suffering becomes a way of dramatizing how Black life is repeatedly denied freedom, safety, and recognition.

Ultimately, the text is a stark indictment of America’s racial and social order. It portrays Black life as trapped within systems that exploit the body, control space, and limit possibility. Through images of violence, predation, and mechanized power, the poem exposes a society that claims to value freedom while denying it to those most oppressed. Its vision is disturbing because it insists that dehumanization is not an exception, but a central feature of systemic racism and social control.
outputs.L5:
Under the flicker of neon lights, the city looked almost holy. Rain glazed the streets, turning every puddle into a stained-glass window of pink, blue, and electric gold. On the corner of an old brick building, a sign buzzed above a closed shop: **JESUS SAVES**, its letters glowing bright against the midnight sky.

Mara stood beneath it, her wrists marked by the memory of chains she had finally broken. They were not made of iron anymore, but of fear, regret, and the voices that told her she would never be free. For years, she had carried them quietly, smiling when she was expected to smile, staying silent when her soul wanted to scream.

But that night, something changed.

The neon hummed like a prayer. The image of Jesus in the window—painted in fading colors, arms open wide—seemed less like a warning and more like an invitation. Mara took a breath, deep and trembling, and let the past fall from her shoulders.

Some chains break loudly. Others dissolve in silence.

She stepped into the glowing street, not knowing exactly where she was going, only that she was no longer willing to remain where she had been. Behind her, the neon sign continued to shine, casting light over the dark pavement like a promise.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a two-part surreal prose poem in the style of 1960s Black Arts poetry, mixing images of landlords, fathers, Christianity, racism, technology, and urban oppression.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. RENT DUE AT THE ALTAR**

The landlord comes wearing my father’s hat, brim low as a Sunday cloud, keys jangling like little police in his fist. He says *son* with a mouth full of eviction notices. He says *the Lord provides* and slides the bill under the door like a pale snake baptized in ink. All night the radiator coughs up psalms. All night the roaches march in formation, tiny deacons of the tenement, carrying crumbs of our hunger to a kingdom behind the stove.

In the hallway, Jesus has been painted white again. His eyes are blue as sirens. His hands glow electric over the cracked plaster, blessing the rats, blessing the rent, blessing the city that eats Black breath and calls it progress. My mother’s Bible opens by itself and the pages turn into pay stubs, then police reports, then maps of neighborhoods cut open by highways. The saints wear hard hats. The angels carry clipboards. The devil is not red—he is administrative, he is mortgage-backed, he is smiling in the bank window with clean fingernails.

Father, where did your thunder go? I hear it trapped in the elevator shaft, rising and falling, rising and falling, never reaching our floor. You told me a man must stand straight, but the ceiling keeps lowering. You told me God watches, but the camera in the lobby watches harder. Its glass eye hums, feeding our faces into a machine that cannot pronounce our names. Somewhere downtown, a computer dreams of us as numbers: debt, risk, suspect, tenant, disposable star.

And still the children chalk suns on the sidewalk. Still old women lean from windows like prophets of steam. Still somebody downstairs beats a drum on an empty paint can, calling the bones back into the body, calling the father back from the factory, calling Black God out of the landlord’s ledger.

**II. MACHINE GOSPEL FOR A BURNING BLOCK**

At midnight the city plugs itself into my spine. Streetlights bloom like cold moons over garbage hills. The subway opens its iron mouth and sings in chains. Beneath the avenue, our grandfathers ride forever, packed shoulder to shoulder with ghosts of cotton fields, ship holds, factories, jail cells, each stop announced by a voice smooth as a white glove: *Next stop: obedience. Next stop: low wages. Next stop: be grateful.*

But we are not grateful. We are neon and ash. We are broken bottle constellations glittering under the boot. We are the black hand pushing back the dawn when dawn comes dressed as a landlord, dressed as a cop, dressed as a preacher selling heaven by the week. The television in the window shows a war, then a commercial, then a choir, then a politician smiling with teeth like apartment gates. The antenna on the roof catches messages from Mars, but none from the mayor.

My father appears in the static, enormous, made of soot and trumpet sound. He says, *Boy, don’t bow to any cross they use as a hammer.* He says, *If God is God, He is not afraid of your rage.* Then his face becomes a circuit board, then a burning bush, then a fist full of stars. I touch the screen and my fingers come away black with newsprint, black with prophecy, black with the night they tried to rename.

The block begins to levitate. Fire escapes unfold into ladders for angels with afros of flame. Parking meters sprout leaves. The church bell turns into a siren turns into a saxophone, and the saxophone screams until every brick remembers who laid it, who paid for it, who was buried beneath it without a stone.

O city, you metal Pharaoh, you concrete beast with a dollar sign branded on your tongue—hear us. We are building a new scripture from noise, rent receipts, busted hymns, and the hot red alphabet of refusal. We are done being shadows in your machine. We are the machine’s nightmare: human, holy, unbought, rising.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem with sections labeled I and II about a Black child watching his father, a predatory landlord, and a city of neon, using violent surrealist imagery and references to America, zebras, IBM, and mad dogs.
counterfactuals.output:
I

The Black child watches his father  
through a window the city has chewed into teeth—  
neon gums, blue spit, a billboard blinking  
AMERICA AMERICA  
like a wound learning to spell.

His father bends over the sink,  
washing rust from his knuckles.  
In the drain: little moons,  
a zebra’s striped skull,  
the rent notice folded into a knife.

Outside, the landlord prowls the stairs  
in a coat of receipts,  
his mouth full of keys and wet thunder.  
He sniffs at doors.  
He names hunger “policy.”  
He names the lock “God.”  
He names the boy’s breath “arrears.”

The child does not move.  
His eyes are two dark radios  
picking up IBM hymns from the towers—  
machines counting every heartbeat,  
sorting grief into columns,  
printing eviction in clean white snow.

Somewhere, mad dogs run through the avenue  
with sirens tied to their tails.  
They bite the streetlights until sparks fall  
like burning insects onto the cars.  
The father looks up once,  
and in that look:  
a whole black ocean lifting its fists,  
a church split open by lightning,  
a zebra galloping out of a hospital  
covered in flags.

II

At midnight the city kneels,  
not to pray,  
but to drink from puddles of gasoline.  
Neon baptizes the alleys pink and green.  
America’s face flickers on every screen—  
powdered, smiling, carnivorous.

The landlord comes again,  
dragging a sack of doorknobs behind him.  
Inside the sack, families whisper.  
Inside the whispers, birds with broken crowns  
beat their wings against ledgers.

The father stands in the hall  
like a match before a storm.  
The child watches.  
The ceiling lowers its antlers.  
The walls sweat coins.  
An IBM moon calculates the damage  
and refuses to weep.

Then the mad dogs arrive—  
red-eyed, star-spangled, holy with foam—  
and the zebras follow,  
striped like crosswalks,  
striped like prison bars,  
striped like the child’s dream of running  
between danger and dawn.

The father raises one hand.  
Not surrender.  
Not blessing.  
Something older than both.

And the city, enormous and neon,  
opens its iron mouth  
to swallow them—

but the child’s gaze becomes a blade of black glass,  
and for one bright second  
every landlord key melts,  
every machine forgets its numbers,  
every dog lies down trembling,  
and America hears, from the basement of its name,  
a boy breathing fire into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, politically charged prose poem that sounds like Amiri Baraka or early radical African American modernism, with themes of rent, poverty, racial exploitation, religion, and mechanized society.
counterfactuals.output:
The landlord’s hand comes through the wall  
before morning—  
a pale machine with a receipt for a tongue,  
knocking, knocking,  
while the babies sleep under coats  
and the radiator coughs up its last rusted prayer.

Rent is the hymn of the city,  
sung in the office of men who own no winter,  
men with soft shoes and policemen in their pockets,  
men who have never heard a mother  
count pennies like bones on a table.

In the church basement,  
the saints eat government cheese  
beneath a picture of a blue-eyed heaven.  
The preacher says suffer now,  
glory later—  
but the rats in the wall got glory tonight,  
fat with our bread,  
holy with our hunger.

O America, iron choir,  
your factories grind the names off our fathers.  
Your clocks punch holes in our backs.  
Your trains drag the dawn across black neighborhoods  
and leave smoke where music used to stand.  
Every piston says work.  
Every siren says run.  
Every bank window says no  
in a voice polished clean as a judge’s gavel.

We are the dark rent due  
on the nation’s bright lie.  
We are the unpaid heat,  
the shutoff notice,  
the hand-me-down blood,  
the storefront prophets crying fire  
while the neon gods blink SALE SALE SALE  
over the bodies of the poor.

And still, somewhere under the elevated tracks,  
a horn splits the night open—  
not pretty, not safe,  
a wounded brass animal  
calling the people by their real names.

Rise, it says.  
Not to heaven.  
Here.  
In the street.  
Where the landlord can see you.  
Where the machines can hear you.  
Where God, if God is more than a locked door,  
must come down hungry  
and stand with us  
against the rent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde urban nightmare poem where a landlord becomes a monstrous symbol, the father is trapped by religion and capitalism, and America is imagined as a zoo full of machines and rabid dogs.
counterfactuals.output:
**LANDLORD BESTIARY**

The landlord grows antlers of eviction notices,  
his mouth a mail slot for bad news,  
his hands—two padlocks blooming in winter.  

He stands in the stairwell  
like a saint of mildew and rent hikes,  
breathing boiler-smoke,  
counting our heartbeats  
as billable utilities.  

In the basement, Father kneels  
between a crucifix and a cash register,  
one eye nailed to heaven,  
the other audited by the bank.  

He prays in coins.  
He bleeds in invoices.  
His Bible has teeth marks  
from the wolves of industry.  

Every Sunday, the sermon is foreclosure.  
Every Monday, the factory whistles  
like a god with a metal throat.  

And America—  
America is a zoo at midnight,  
cages stacked to the horizon,  
turnstiles clicking like insects.  

The elephants are bulldozers.  
The birds are surveillance drones.  
The lions have engines  
instead of lungs.  

In the monkey house, executives  
throw contracts at one another  
and shriek beneath fluorescent suns.  

Rabid dogs patrol the gift shop,  
foam-bright, flag-striped,  
trained to bite the poor  
and lick the boots of uniforms.  

The children feed quarters  
to the vending machines,  
and the vending machines  
feed back tiny plastic graves.  

O landlord, tower of bone and paperwork,  
o beast with a lease for a tongue,  
you climb the skyline  
wearing our windows as eyes.  

Father cannot escape the chapel  
because the chapel is mortgaged.  
He cannot escape the market  
because the market has learned to sing hymns.  

Above us, the city shakes  
its iron fur.  
Below us, the pipes cough up black communion.  

We sleep in rented shadows,  
dreaming of bolt cutters,  
while the zoo gates open inward  
and the dogs begin to laugh.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, hallucinatory poem in two numbered sections about Black suffering in America, using images of cotton, neon, spiders, operating tables, Jesus’ blood, zebras, and IBM computers.
counterfactuals.output:
1.

Cotton blooms like a white fever in the mouth of the field,  
each boll a small skull whispering *pick me, pick me*  
under a neon moon that buzzes like a bad transformer.  
Grandmothers bend into the weather, their backs  
written over by ledgers, auction bells, courthouse dust—  
and from the rafters of history, spiders lower themselves,  
black stars on silk threads, sewing wounds shut  
with the same needles that opened them.

On the operating table of America, the body keeps singing.  
A blue glove enters the dream. A scalpel flashes  
like a sheriff’s badge. Someone says *progress*  
and the cotton turns red in the basin.  
Jesus’ blood drips from a cracked billboard beside the highway,  
mixing with rain, oil, and the last hymn  
a boy ever heard before the sirens flowered.

Somewhere, zebras run through a burning avenue—  
striped as prison bars, striped as crosswalks,  
striped as the static on a television after the verdict.  
Their hooves strike sparks from the asphalt.  
Their eyes are huge with the knowledge  
that even miracles can be hunted.

2.

In the basement of the century, IBM computers hum  
like cold choirs, counting names into numbers,  
numbers into policy, policy into cages,  
cages into neighborhoods where neon liquor signs  
flicker *open* all night above the closed future.  
The machine dreams in punch cards and census tracts,  
in mortgages denied, in maps red as cauterized flesh.

Spiders build cathedrals inside the circuitry.  
Cotton lint drifts through the vents like ancestral snow.  
On the operating table, the patient is still breathing—  
America masked and gloved, America asking  
where it hurts while pressing down harder.

Jesus’ blood is not metaphor here:  
it is in the sink, the street, the cotton root,  
the mother’s sleeve, the ambulance sheet,  
the song that refuses to die though every century  
has tried to cut out its tongue.

And the zebras return at dawn, impossible and luminous,  
grazing among the ruined terminals,  
their stripes rearranging into rivers, fingerprints,  
barcodes, piano keys, roadways north—  
a living black-and-white prophecy  
breaking from the lab, the ledger, the noose,  
running past the neon, past the cotton,  
past the spiders’ patient silver grammar,  
toward a sun no machine can number.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
